passage:
"So? How was week six?" Lokesh asked, reaching for the papad.
"Actually good," Meenal said. "Ritesh sir and I have a Monday check-in now. Fifteen minutes. And he wrote down what a finished report should look like. One page."
"The same Ritesh who embarrassed you in front of everyone?" Appa put down his spoon.
"Same one. After I asked to talk privately, things changed. He even said my question list was useful."
"You went and told your boss how to give feedback?" Lokesh grinned. "Brave."
"I didn't tell him. I asked. Politely."
Her father, Shankar, nodded slowly. "When I was young, I would have just stayed angry for a year."
"I almost did, Appa. It was worse."

qa.q: How long is Meenal's Monday check-in?
What does Meenal's 'I almost did, Appa. It was worse' suggest she has learned?
qa.a: She seems to feel that swallowing her anger was more painful than speaking up, and she's relieved she chose to raise it.

qa.q: Which working habits helped Meenal and Ritesh sir move forward?
qa.a: A short weekly check-in and a written description of a finished report, which replaced guessing with clear expectations.

qa.q: How does Shankar seem to see his daughter's approach?
qa.a: He seems impressed and a little reflective, comparing it with how he would have stayed angry for a year when he was young.

grounding: At dinner a young woman tells her family how a weekly check-in and written expectations followed her respectful complaint, building trust with her senior.

passage: Three months into my internship, I, Leela, finally understand what happened with Chetan. For weeks I'd been the quiet new girl, sitting on my resentment: the public corrections, the one-word emails. After we talked privately, we tried something simple. Every Friday at four, ten minutes at his desk. And a shared document titled 'What done looks like', where he wrote the standard for every task before I started it. The first Friday felt stiff. By the fourth, I was bringing my own list of questions, and he was asking what I thought. Last week he disagreed with my plan, and I said, 'I see it differently,' out loud, in a meeting. He said, 'Good point, let's try yours.' Swallowing it never got me that. Saying it respectfully did.

qa.q: What was the shared document titled?
qa.a: It was titled 'What done looks like'.

qa.q: How did Leela feel during the first Friday check-in compared with the fourth?
qa.a: The first felt stiff and awkward, but by the fourth she felt confident enough to bring her own questions, suggesting growing trust.

qa.q: Why did the weekly check-in and shared document help?
qa.a: They made expectations clear before work began and gave a regular, safe place to raise problems, so resentment didn't build up.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Leela now compared with before?
qa.a: He probably sees her as a contributor whose views are worth hearing, since he now asks her opinion and accepted her plan.

grounding: A young woman looks back on how a weekly check-in and written standards turned swallowed resentment into respectful disagreement and trust.
